method: Old skill against new, three runs per arm, each run doing the three cases in one session from a scratch directory, arms named neutrally (s1, s2). One blind Opus judge scored every rubric item 0/1, a 1-5 'reads like a person' score, and any dropped fact. The skill changed before the cases were written and was not edited after the runs, except sources.md (documentation only). q05 resembles the owner's real example that prompted the change, so its gain is partly by construction. Outputs and scores are kept outside the repository. Round 2 ran on the final files: q07 and q08 written fresh after the openings rule and before any run, q04 and q05 re-run as a regression check, same arms, models and blind judge; q06 was not re-run because the rule was written in answer to it.
notes: q05: every old run dropped the stapled notarization ticket and two said 'without a network/internet connection'; one wrongly said Apple signed the DMG; every new run kept every fact and 'even when you're offline' (the detail rule and inline example did it). q04: indistinguishable on rubric, new slightly more human and dropped nothing. q06: worse; all six runs in both arms opened on 'Tidepool takes a snapshot' instead of the reader's moment, and new runs more often missed stating what the guide lets the reader do; nothing in the change addresses a guide's opening, so lead-with-the-reader's-moment for guides is the next gap. Round 2: the new skill scored higher on all four cases and dropped no fact on q04 or q05 (old dropped 8); on the fresh openings, 1 of 3 new runs per case opened from the reader's moment against 0 of 3 old, so the opening rule moves the result only part of the time; q04's 'human' score fell from 4.67 to 4.0 while its rubric rose; four old and some new shiftdb openings gave the tool a mind ('so it knows').
